stops.name: Brooklyn, the birth
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day and invariant across sources: Wikipedia, 'Bob Kahn', gives 23 December 1938, Brooklyn, New York, parents Lawrence and Beatrice Pauline Kahn, an Ashkenazi Jewish family. No source consulted names the hospital or the neighborhood within the borough, and none claims to. The coordinate is the Brooklyn centroid and stands for a borough, not for a building.
stops.campa: Robert Elliot Kahn is born in Brooklyn on the twenty-third of December, 1938, to Lawrence and Beatrice Pauline Kahn. The family is Ashkenazi Jewish, and the borough is the whole of what the record gives: no source consulted names the hospital, and none names the street. He will spend his working life on the question of how a message crosses ground it cannot see. The coordinate here is the Brooklyn centroid, standing for a borough rather than for a door.

stops.name: City College of New York, the engineering degree
stops.date_confidence: Attested year, defaulted month and day: Wikipedia, 'Bob Kahn', gives a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from City College of New York in 1960. June is a commencement default and is not sourced. The coordinate is the Convent Avenue campus in Harlem, which is the only City College campus the sources name.
stops.campa: Kahn takes a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from City College of New York, on the Convent Avenue campus in Harlem, the free municipal college that has been turning the children of immigrants into engineers for a century. He is twenty-one. Forty-five years later the college's alumni association will bring him back to this same campus to hang the Townsend Harris Medal on him, and by then the network he built will be carrying the mail of the world. Between the two visits he does not appear on this coordinate at all.
suggested_refs: City College of New York, Convent Avenue campus, bachelor's degree 1960 and Townsend Harris Medal 2005

stops.name: Murray Hill, the technical staff at Bell Laboratories
stops.date_confidence: Employment attested, date and site reconstructed. Which Bell Labs site held him is unrecorded in anything reached; Murray Hill is a guess and is marked as one. Holmdel and Whippany are equally available.
stops.campa: Between the City College degree and the Princeton doctorate, Kahn works on the technical staff at Bell Telephone Laboratories, the industrial research house that has already produced the transistor and information theory itself. CNRI's own account of his life states the employment plainly and gives it no dates. Which of the Bell sites held him is not recorded anywhere reached; Murray Hill is the guess and is marked as one. He is in his early twenties. No packet network exists anywhere in the world.

stops.name: Princeton, the master's degree
stops.date_confidence: Attested year, defaulted month and day: Wikipedia, 'Bob Kahn', gives a Master of Arts in electrical engineering from Princeton University in 1962, with Bede Liu as doctoral advisor. The coordinate is the Engineering Quadrangle, named in the research pool's geography lens; no source places him in a particular room or laboratory.
stops.campa: Kahn takes a Master of Arts in electrical engineering at Princeton, in the Engineering Quadrangle, and stays on for the doctorate. He is twenty-three. He works under Bede Liu on the mathematics of signals: how a wave that is continuous in time can be cut into samples, carried as pieces, and made whole again at the other end. Nothing in the subject touches computers. Two years remain on the doctorate, and he spends them on waveforms rather than on messages.
suggested_refs: Princeton University Engineering Quadrangle, where Kahn worked under Bede Liu

stops.name: Princeton, some problems in the sampling and modulation of signals
stops.date_confidence: Attested year and title, defaulted month and day: Wikipedia, 'Bob Kahn', gives the PhD in electrical engineering at Princeton in 1964 with the dissertation title 'Some problems in the sampling and modulation of signals.' The date of the defense is not recorded in any source reached; June is a default.
stops.campa: The doctorate is granted in 1964. The dissertation is titled 'Some problems in the sampling and modulation of signals,' and it is about the cutting of a continuous thing into discrete pieces that can be carried and reassembled. Nine years later he will be performing the same operation on messages instead of waveforms, and calling the pieces packets. He leaves Princeton for a teaching post in Cambridge. There is no ARPANET yet, and no contract has been let to build one.
suggested_refs: Kahn's Princeton dissertation, 'Some problems in the sampling and modulation of signals,' 1964

stops.name: MIT, the assistant professorship
stops.date_confidence: Appointment attested, dates reconstructed. CNRI's institutional biography states that Kahn 'became an Assistant Professor of Electrical Engineering at MIT'; the research pool's two lenses both tagged this [R] and both under-claimed it, one dating it 1966 and one c. 1964 to 1966. CNRI and the standard accounts have him at MIT from roughly 1964 and taking leave in 1966 for BBN, so 1966 is a departure year, not a start. September 1964 is an academic-year default. The coordinate is MIT's main campus and is confirmed correct by the pool.
stops.campa: Kahn becomes an Assistant Professor of Electrical Engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. CNRI's institutional biography states the appointment; the years around it are reconstruction. He teaches for about two years and then takes leave, meaning to spend a season in industry and come back. He does not come back. The leave runs to the end of his working life, and the industry he steps into is a small acoustics consultancy across the river that has just been handed a contract to build a network.
suggested_refs: MIT Department of Electrical Engineering, the professorship Kahn took leave from in 1966 and never resumed

stops.name: Cambridge, 10 Moulton Street
stops.date_confidence: Role attested, year reconstructed. Wikipedia, 'Bob Kahn', confirms that he worked at Bolt Beranek and Newman as principal designer on the ARPANET, but its Career section gives no year at all: it says only that 'Kahn first worked at Bolt Beranek and Newman Inc.' The 1966 date comes from elsewhere and is carried as reconstruction; month and day are defaults. The address is corrected: BBN's Cambridge headquarters, the IMP building, was 10 Moulton Street, not the 50 Moulton Street the research pool gave. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical BBN pin, inherited byte-identical from vint_cerf.journey.json, stop 'Cambridge, the working group at BBN'.
stops.campa: Bolt Beranek and Newman occupies a low brick building at 10 Moulton Street, and Kahn arrives as a man on leave from a professorship. He becomes principal designer on the ARPANET and writes much of the technical proposal that wins BBN the contract to build the Interface Message Processors, the machines that will sit between each host computer and the network. Vint Cerf's own record of this same building remembers it differently, as host of the Network Working Group, a stop where Kahn goes unnamed even though the two men's collaboration is only a few years off.
suggested_refs: Bolt Beranek and Newman, 10 Moulton Street, Cambridge, and the Interface Message Processor proposal

stops.name: Boelter Hall, the first node
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month: the first ARPANET node was installed at UCLA in September 1969, and Wikipedia's articles on Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn both place their meeting at UCLA in this period. The day is a default. Kahn's own physical presence in Boelter Hall on the installation date is not attested; what is attested is that he worked on the system architecture and that the two men met here. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Boelter Hall pin, inherited byte-identical from vint_cerf.journey.json, in preference to the research pool's 34.0689, -118.4432.
stops.campa: The first Interface Message Processor is installed at UCLA in Boelter Hall, and the network Kahn helped specify becomes a thing with one node. He is here on the architecture, and here he meets a young engineer named Vint Cerf, whose own path through this same institution starts at this same coordinate. They will spend the next decade writing the rules by which one kind of network speaks to another kind. The machine in the room is a Honeywell minicomputer with no screen.
suggested_refs: Boelter Hall 3420, UCLA, site of the first ARPANET Interface Message Processor

stops.name: SRI International, the second node
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: Wikipedia, 'History of the Internet', gives 29 October 1969 for the first host-to-host message from UCLA to SRI, the second ARPANET node. Kahn's presence at SRI on that day is not attested and is not claimed here; the stop marks the network his architecture work underlies reaching two nodes. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical SRI pin, shared byte-identical with vint_cerf.journey.json.
stops.campa: The second node goes live at the Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, and on the twenty-ninth of October the first host-to-host message crosses from UCLA to this building. Two nodes make a network. The architecture Kahn worked on at BBN now has something to carry. Eight years later, almost to the month, a van belonging to this same institute will drive a California freeway with a radio in it and prove that three networks of entirely different kinds can be made to behave as one.
suggested_refs: SRI International, 333 Ravenswood Avenue, Menlo Park, second ARPANET node

stops.name: The Hilton Washington, twenty computers in a hotel
stops.date_confidence: Attested in date, venue, and Kahn's organizing role: Wikipedia's article on the International Conference on Computer Communications gives 24 to 26 October 1972 at the Hilton Washington, organised by BBN under Kahn's direction with Larry Roberts as conference chair. Two corrections to the research pool are carried here. The number of machines is 20, per Wikipedia 'Bob Kahn', the Internet Hall of Fame biography, and the pool's own chronology lens; the pool's geography lens said 'some forty' and is wrong. The pool's coordinates 38.9207, -77.0431 fall roughly 500 m northeast of the hotel and are replaced.
stops.campa: At the International Conference on Computer Communications, held at the Hilton Washington from the twenty-fourth to the twenty-sixth of October, Kahn organizes the first public demonstration of the ARPANET: twenty computers, wired into a hotel, answering strangers. Larry Roberts chairs the conference; BBN runs the floor under Kahn's direction. It is afterward called the event that convinced the skeptics packet switching was real and not a research paper. He is thirty-three, and it is the last thing he does for BBN.
suggested_refs: The 1972 International Conference on Computer Communications at the Hilton Washington, first public ARPANET demonstration
sources: Internet Hall of Fame, inductee biography of Robert Kahn

stops.name: Arlington, the Information Processing Techniques Office
stops.date_confidence: Attested year, defaulted month and day: Wikipedia, 'Bob Kahn', has him moving from BBN to DARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office in 1972 and working on the SATNET satellite packet project, where he develops the initial concepts of the Transmission Control Protocol. November is placed after the October ICCC demonstration and is a narrative default, not a sourced month. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical DARPA Arlington pin from vint_cerf.journey.json, used in preference to the research pool's 38.8956, -77.0715.
stops.campa: Kahn crosses from the contractor's side to the government's, joining DARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office in Arlington. He is given the satellite packet project, SATNET, and finds himself holding three networks that work in three incompatible ways: a wired one, a radio one, and one that goes through the sky. Nothing joins them. The initial concepts of what will be called the Transmission Control Protocol are worked out here, in an office building, by a man who now funds the work instead of doing it.
suggested_refs: DARPA Information Processing Techniques Office, Arlington, and the SATNET satellite packet program

stops.date_confidence: Attested in substance, defaulted in date. Wikipedia, 'Bob Kahn', has Cerf joining the internetworking project in 1973; vint_cerf.journey.json, stop 'Stanford, the assistant professorship', states plainly that 'Robert Kahn brings him the problem directly from DARPA' and dates that stop 1972-09-01. stops.campa: Kahn carries the internetworking problem to Stanford and puts it in front of Vint Cerf, newly an assistant professor there, fresh from his own work on the ARPANET's host-to-host protocol. Cerf's own account of the moment holds it in a single line: Robert Kahn brings him the problem directly from DARPA. The two men begin here, on this campus, the collaboration that will define the rest of both their careers and give the network its addressing scheme.

Whether Kahn is in the room himself is not attested; Cerf's presence is, and the stop marks the idea rather than the man's body in it.

stops.name: Stanford, the paper that names the gateway
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the issue: Cerf and Kahn, 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication,' IEEE Transactions on Communications COM-22 no. 5, May 1974, pp. 637 to 648. The PDF was fetched and read directly during the research pass and the quotations here are verbatim from it. The day is a default within the issue month. The research pool notes that the IEEE Xplore issue metadata was not independently re-fetched. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Stanford pin, which vint_cerf.journey.json already uses for this same paper.
stops.campa: In the May 1974 issue of IEEE Transactions on Communications, Cerf and Kahn publish 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication.' It defines a host, defines a packet switch, and then defines the thing that had no name: the box standing between two networks that speak differently, which they call a gateway. The paper runs thirteen pages and outlives every piece of hardware it describes. Every router now on earth is a descendant of a word coined on page 638.
stops.quote: It is thus apparent that the interface between networks must play a central role in the development of any network interconnection strategy. We give a special name to this interface that performs these functions and call it a GATEWAY.
stops.quote_source: Vinton G. Cerf and Robert E. Kahn, 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication,' IEEE Transactions on Communications, vol. COM-22 no. 5, May 1974, p. 638
suggested_refs: Cerf and Kahn, 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication,' IEEE Trans. Comm. COM-22 no. 5, May 1974, pp. 637-648

stops.campa: In December the first full specification of the Transmission Control Program is issued as RFC 675, written by Cerf with Yogen Dalal and Carl Sunshine. Kahn does not sign it. He appears in the acknowledgments, thanked among those who supplied good ideas and counsel, which is the documentary trace a program director leaves: his name in the thanks and not on the byline. The paper of May is now a specification a programmer can build from, and the building begins.
stops.quote: This document describes the functions to be performed by the internetwork Transmission Control Program [TCP] and its interface to programs or users that require its services.
stops.quote_source: Vinton Cerf, Yogen Dalal, and Carl Sunshine, RFC 675, 'Specification of Internet Transmission Control Program,' December 1974, opening sentence

Wikipedia, 'History of the Internet', reads: 'On November 22, 1977, a three network demonstration was conducted including the ARPANET, the SRI's Packet Radio Van on the Packet Radio Network and the Atlantic Packet Satellite Network (SATNET) including a node at UCL.' Not confirmed by that or any source reached: the Bayshore Freeway as the van's route, and the figure of roughly ninety-four thousand miles round trip without a lost bit. stops.campa: On the twenty-second of November a van fitted with packet radio drives a freeway south of San Francisco and puts packets into the air. They cross the Packet Radio Network, the ARPANET, and the Atlantic Packet Satellite Network, three networks built by different people for different purposes, and arrive intact. The demonstration is the proof of the 1974 paper. The route is traditionally given as the Bayshore Freeway and the round trip as ninety-four thousand miles; neither figure is in any source reached.

No primary technical account reached this session names Goonhilly for the twenty-second of November. The pin stands on the tradition and is marked as tradition. What is attested is that a satellite hop is in the loop and that a node in London sits on the far side of it.

The packets that left a van on a California freeway travel over satellite, land line and radio before they reach Gower Street and turn around. Vint Cerf's own account of the same demonstration calls this stop the far leg; Kahn's connection to the place is the money and the architecture behind it, not his body in the room.

stops.name: Arlington, the protocol splits in two
stops.date_confidence: Attested year, no attested place or month. Wikipedia, 'Bob Kahn', dates to 1978 the splitting of the Transmission Control Protocol into TCP for host-to-host transport and IP for internetwork addressing and routing. No source reached names a location for the decision, and the design work is distributed across Stanford, DARPA, BBN, and elsewhere. The DARPA pin is an administrative placement, not a room where it happened, and month and day are defaults.
stops.campa: The Transmission Control Protocol is cut in half. What is left as TCP handles the conversation between two hosts; what is taken out becomes IP and handles only addressing and routing across networks, knowing nothing about the conversation it carries. The split is the reason the thing scales, because a network that must be told nothing can be joined by anyone. No ceremony marks it and no location is attested. The pin is the DARPA office, an administrative placement and not a room.
suggested_refs: The 1978 separation of TCP from IP, the layering that made the internet joinable without permission

stops.name: Arlington, the director's office
stops.date_confidence: Attested year, defaulted month and day: Wikipedia, 'Bob Kahn', has him becoming director of DARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office in 1979. The same source's awards list gives his election as an IEEE Fellow in 1981; no ceremony, city, or venue is recorded for that anywhere reached, which is why it is folded into this stop rather than given a pin of its own. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical DARPA Arlington pin.
stops.campa: Kahn becomes director of the Information Processing Techniques Office, the DARPA post that has funded almost everything in American computing since Licklider held it. He will be made an IEEE Fellow two years later, and no ceremony for that is recorded anywhere reached. From this desk he now decides what gets built. The protocol he co-designed is still a research system running on a few hundred machines, and the decision to make it the network's only language has not yet been taken.
suggested_refs: The DARPA IPTO directorship, 1979, and the IEEE Fellowship of 1981 with no recorded ceremony

stops.name: Arlington, Flag Day
stops.date_confidence: The event is attested to the day; Kahn's personal presence is not. On 1 January 1983 the Network Control Program was switched off across the ARPANET and TCP/IP became mandatory. vint_cerf.journey.json, stop 'Arlington, Flag Day', states that DARPA Arlington is the administrative center for the cutover and that no ceremonial site is documented, and it does not attest anyone's presence on the day. That hedge is carried here unchanged.
stops.campa: On the first of January the older Network Control Program is switched off across the ARPANET and TCP/IP becomes the only way to speak on it. Machines that have not converted go silent. It is remembered as flag day, and it is the moment the protocol Kahn and Cerf wrote stops being an experiment and becomes the floor. Cerf's file records that DARPA Arlington administers the cutover and that no ceremonial site is documented; whether Kahn is at his desk that morning is attested nowhere.
suggested_refs: The TCP/IP flag day of 1 January 1983, when NCP was switched off across the ARPANET

He is chairman, chief executive, and president, and he will still hold all three titles thirty-six years later. Vint Cerf joins him here as vice president in the same year, the first time since 1972 that the two men are inside one institution.

stops.name: Reston, the National Information Infrastructure
stops.date_confidence: The coinage is attested; the year is not. The Internet Hall of Fame's inductee biography of Robert Kahn states that he 'coined the term National Information Infrastructure (NII) in the mid 1980s' and gives nothing narrower. The research pool tagged 1986 as attested to that source, which the source does not support; the year here is a placement inside a range and the month is a default chosen only to sit after the CNRI founding. No evidence orders the two events.
stops.campa: Kahn coins the term National Information Infrastructure for the thing he is trying to get built: a public network fabric on which anything at all can be carried. The press shortens it to the Information Super Highway, and it is the shortened version that gets famous and then gets mocked, while the phrase Kahn wrote stays inside the policy documents. The Internet Hall of Fame dates the coinage only to the mid 1980s; no source reached gives a year, and the year printed here is a placement inside a range.
suggested_refs: Internet Hall of Fame inductee biography of Robert Kahn, on the coinage of National Information Infrastructure
